meta.blurb: Your attention is a small bag of coins, and Maya spends hers on every email, opinion and plan. She is exhausted. This short, honest guide helps you choose the few things worth the struggle, and let the rest go.
meta.bible: Maya: a busy office worker who cares about everything and is tired. Leo: her younger cousin, learning the guitar. Sam: Maya's friend who often cancels plans. Dev: Maya's colleague, who sends messages all day. Ines: Maya's manager, fair and direct. Ms Okafor: Leo's guitar teacher. Mr Haddad: an elderly neighbour who used to repair clocks. Rob: a former colleague who once presented Maya's idea as his own. Mr Lam: the teacher of the evening painting class Maya joins. Aunt Nora: Leo's mother and Maya's aunt, who ran a small corner shop for thirty years. The book speaks to You in plain, kind, slightly humorous words. Key terms: Attention, Coins, Values, Boundaries, Struggle, Control, Responsibility, Feedback, Commitment. Voice: warm, direct, practical and honest, never harsh. No invented studies or numbers. This is not a book about not caring: it is about choosing what to care about. The book is in twenty chapters of ten pages and ends with Maya choosing where her coins go.

Maya decides to try something new, and she buys a small notebook.
Leo wants to play the guitar well, so he must practise a lot.
Every good thing has a price, so you must choose your struggle.
The easy path is flat, but the steep path has a better view.
Do not only ask what you want, but what pain you accept.
If you will not accept the struggle, you do not really want the goal.
Leo's fingers hurt after practice, but he plays again the next day.
Maya wants to be fit, but she does not like early mornings.
A better job pays more money, but it also takes more time.
Some hard things feel good, because you chose them yourself.

A bad feeling is normal, and it is a signal, not an order.
Before her talk, Maya's heart beats fast and she wants to run away.
Many people feel bad about feeling bad, and this makes it worse.
Sometimes you feel bad because you are tired or hungry.

Think of a day when you felt happy and like yourself.

A value is a direction, and you never finish walking it.
Sort your worries into things you can control and things you cannot.

You cannot control what happens, but you can choose your answer.
The train is late, so Maya reads a book instead.
You cannot choose what other people think about you.
Maya cannot control the answer, but she can prepare well.

Knowing that life ends can help us choose what matters.
From far away, many of our worries look very small.
Maya calls an old friend that she has not seen for years.
Maya plans one important thing for this week.

B1B2: Imagine that you wake up each morning with a small bag of coins. Those coins are your attention, and everything you notice, worry about or care about costs you some of them.
Caring is never free, and it costs you a little more than you expect. When you care about your work, your friends, the news and your looks, each one asks for a share of your day.
Most of us try to care about everything at once. We want to be good at work, popular with friends, healthy, rich and well informed, and by the evening we feel completely empty.
Meet Maya, who works in an office and answers every email within minutes. She also follows every headline and worries about what each colleague thinks of her, and she is always exhausted.
One evening Maya writes down everything she paid attention to that day. The list is long, and she is shocked to see how much of it does not matter to her.
Her colleague Dev sends a message every few minutes, and Maya answers each one immediately. She tells herself that this is being helpful, although she never finishes her own work.
When the evening comes, Maya is exhausted, yet she cannot name one thing she achieved today. She was busy from morning until night, but almost none of it was something she chose.
Choosing what to care about does not make you cold or selfish. A cold person cares about nothing, but a wise person cares about a few things very deeply.
Nobody can stop caring completely, because we are made to notice things. The real question is not whether you will care but what you will care about.
Maya decides that she cannot go on like this, so she buys a plain notebook. On the first page she writes a promise: from now on, she will choose where her coins go.
Maya's cousin Leo dreams of playing the guitar in front of an audience. What he does not dream about is the practice, the sore fingers and the dull exercises that come first.
Every goal comes with its own kind of pain. A person who wants to be fit accepts tired legs, and a person who wants a calm home accepts difficult conversations.
In the park there are two paths, and one is smooth and flat while the other climbs a rocky hill. Most people take the easy one, yet only the hill gives you a view over the whole city.
Everyone wants a happy life, a good job and a loving family, so wanting is easy. A better question is what you are willing to put up with to get it.
Many people say they want to learn a language, run a race or write a book. If they are never willing to do the dull daily work, the wish is really only a daydream.
Leo's fingertips are sore and red after a week of practice, and he nearly gives up. Then his teacher, Ms Okafor, tells him that the soreness is simply the price of the music.
Maya says she wants to be fit, but she hates getting up early and running in the cold. She loves the idea of the goal, but she has never agreed to pay its price.
Dev wants a promotion, and he is excited about the money and the new title. He has not yet thought about the longer hours, the extra stress and the evenings he will lose.
A baker does not mind burnt loaves, because she loves the work and the learning. The struggle is the same size for everyone, yet it feels lighter when you have chosen it.
In her notebook Maya writes the title Struggles I Accept and lists three things beneath it. The list is short, and for the first time it feels like hers.
Feelings tell you something, but they do not have to tell you what to do. Fear, sadness and anger are normal parts of life, and having them does not mean that something has gone wrong.
Before her presentation, Maya's heart pounds, and every part of her says that she should cancel. She treats the feeling as an order, and she is almost ready to obey it.
Maya feels nervous before a meeting, and then she feels angry with herself for being nervous. Next she worries that the worry will ruin the meeting, and now she has three problems instead of one.
Maya feels hopeless one afternoon and decides that her whole life must be wrong. Then she eats a sandwich and drinks some water, and the world looks a little kinder.
Try this instead: say quietly that you feel nervous, and let the feeling stay for a while. Feelings that are not fought against often rise, peak and fade by themselves.
Maya tries a small trick and tells herself quietly that she is nervous. Giving the feeling a name makes it clearer, and it seems less like a storm and more like a visitor.
Maya notices that the dread she felt at noon has almost gone by four o'clock. Feelings are weather, not buildings, and they keep moving as long as you let them.
An email from a client makes Maya furious, and her fingers are already typing a sharp reply. Instead she closes the laptop, goes for a walk, and decides to answer tomorrow.
It is not only bad feelings that can mislead us, because happy ones can do it too. Maya feels a rush of joy in a shop, buys an expensive jacket, and has forgotten it by the weekend.

Maya makes a habit of asking herself three things: what she feels, what it is telling her, and what she will choose to do. If a low mood lasts for weeks, it is wise to talk to a doctor or a trusted person.
Values are the standards by which you decide whether your life is going well. Some values are poor choices, such as always being liked or always being richer than your neighbour.
Dev has a rule that he must always be right, and he argues over every small thing. He wins many arguments, but he loses a little of his friends' warmth each time.
Maya looks at her calendar and her bank statement and asks what they say about her values. They say that she values speed, approval and being busy, which is not what she would have chosen.
Better values are the ones you can live out on your own, such as honesty, curiosity, kindness and effort. Nobody can take them away from you, and you do not need anyone's permission to practise them.
Mr Haddad is an elderly neighbour who used to repair clocks, and today his shopping bags are heavy. Maya carries them up the steps, and she feels more like herself than she has all week.
Here is a simple test for any value: can you live by it today, even if nobody notices and nobody helps? If the answer is yes, it is probably a good one to build your life on.
Leo used to dream of being famous, but fame is not something he can practise today. He decides instead to play as well as he can for whoever is in the room.
Maya remembers three days when she felt most like herself and asks what they had in common. Each one involved making something, helping someone or telling the truth.
Maya chooses three words for her card, which are honest, useful and curious. She knows that her values may change a little over the years, so she will read the card again each season.
A goal is a place you can reach, but a value is a direction you keep walking in. You can finish a report, yet you can never finish being honest.
Take a sheet of paper and draw two circles, one for what you control and one for the rest. Your effort and your words go in the first, while the weather and other people's opinions go in the second.
Maya lists her worries and sorts them, putting her sleep and her replies in the small circle. The traffic, her manager's mood and the news all go in the large one.
You cannot decide whether it rains, but you can decide whether you take an umbrella. Life works in much the same way, because you choose your response even when you cannot choose the event.
The morning train is forty minutes late, and Maya cannot make it come any faster. She stops checking the board, opens a book, and decides that the delay is hers to use.
Maya sees two colleagues whispering and immediately wonders if they are talking about her. Then she remembers that their opinions belong in the large circle, and her own behaviour in the small one.
Maya cannot decide whether her audience will clap or yawn. She can decide how well she prepares, so she practises her talk twice in an empty room.
Suppose a storm blows your neighbour's tree onto your fence. It is not your fault, but it is now your problem, because nobody else is going to fix it for you.
A glass slips from the tray in the office kitchen, and it is not Maya's fault. Somebody must sweep it up before someone is hurt, and she is the one who is there.
Blaming other people can feel good for a moment, but it leaves you waiting for them to change. When you take responsibility, even for something that was not your fault, you can start acting today.
Sam cancels another dinner at the last minute, and this is not Maya's fault. How she responds is her own responsibility, so she decides to think about it first.
It feels good to be certain, because certainty means you can stop thinking. The trouble is that all of us hold some beliefs that are mistaken, and we rarely know which ones they are.
Leo believes he is simply bad at maths and always will be. When Maya asks him what would happen if he were wrong, he admits that nobody ever explained fractions to him properly.
Maya has always said, very firmly, that she is not a creative person. When she asks herself why she believes it, she remembers one unkind comment from a school teacher.
Maya starts asking herself a question whenever she feels very sure, which is what she would see if she were wrong. The question is uncomfortable, but it has already saved her from two bad arguments.
You do not have to change your mind all at once. Pick a belief you doubt a little, try the opposite for a month, and write down what actually happens.
Maya asks Dev why he disagrees with her, and then she simply listens. She does not agree with all of it, but she learns two things she had never considered.
Most of us have firm opinions about countries, diets and money that we have never studied. Often they come from a headline we read quickly, or from something a friend once said.
In a meeting Maya is asked a question that she cannot answer, and she says plainly that she does not know. Nobody laughs, and Ines thanks her for being honest about it.
Maya used to think that changing her mind meant losing an argument. Now she sees it as a sign that she is still learning, and she even enjoys saying that she has been wrong.
For one month Maya draws something small for ten minutes every evening. At the end she looks at the pile of pages and admits that she was wrong about not being creative.
Nobody learns to ride a bicycle without falling off at least once. We accept this for children, yet we expect ourselves to be perfect on the first attempt in everything we do as adults.
Ms Okafor shows Leo her old practice notebook, which is full of crossed-out lines and angry notes. Every expert, she says, was once a beginner who failed many times.
On Thursday evening Maya stands outside the painting class with her coat still on. She can hear laughter inside, and she is more nervous than she was before her talk.
Maya is afraid to join a painting class because she might be bad at it. When she decides that success simply means turning up and learning something, the fear loses much of its power.
Mr Lam asks everyone to paint an apple, and Maya's looks more like a potato. She laughs, and to her surprise the evening is one of the best of her month.
At a family dinner Leo plays a wrong chord, and his face turns red. He takes a breath, finds the right chord and carries on, and nobody remembers the mistake except him.
We feel as though everyone is watching our mistakes, but most people are busy thinking about themselves. Hardly anyone spends as much time on your slip as you do.
When something goes wrong, Maya writes down three things: what happened, what it taught her, and what she will try next. She does not blame herself, because the point is to learn and not to punish.
Maya decides to try new things where failure is cheap, such as a recipe or a quick sketch. A burnt dinner costs very little, and it teaches her something each time.
Mr Lam studies Maya's painting for a long time and points to one bright corner. He tells her that this is where she stopped worrying, and that it is the best part.
We often wait to feel ready before we start, but it usually works the other way round. Do something tiny, and the feeling of wanting to continue tends to arrive afterwards.
If a task feels too big, promise yourself just five minutes of it. You are allowed to stop when the time is up, but you will often find that you want to carry on.
Maya's plan to get fit, learn to paint and tidy her flat feels exciting for one evening. By the next morning it seems so huge and vague that she does nothing at all.
Maya makes her first steps laughably small, such as one stretch, one sentence or one minute of tidying. They are so easy that her mind has no excuse to refuse.
Maya attaches her new habit to something she already does every day, which is making her morning tea. While the kettle boils, she writes one line in her notebook.
On days when she is exhausted, Maya does the smallest possible version of her habit. A tiny effort keeps the habit alive, and a habit that is alive can grow again tomorrow.
Leo comes home from school exhausted, and an hour of guitar practice sounds quite impossible. He promises himself ten minutes, and when the time is up he is enjoying himself, so he plays on.
Leo has moved his guitar from its dusty case to a stand in the middle of the room. Maya sets out her running shoes the night before, and both of them begin more easily.
Maya hangs a calendar on her wall and puts a small cross on every day that she keeps her habit. The row of crosses grows longer, and she does not want to break the chain.
After two weeks Maya compares her first sketch with her latest one. Nothing dramatic has happened, but the change is clear, and it came from small things done every day.
Each time you say yes to something, you are saying no to something else, because the day has only so many hours. Saying yes to every request means saying no to your own plans.
Maya imagines two doors in a corridor, one marked yes and one marked no. For years she has walked through the yes door without looking, while her own plans waited behind the other one.
In one week Maya agrees to help Dev with a report, join a committee for Ines and mind a neighbour's cat. Her calendar is full, and not one of the things on it is hers.
Saying no does not have to be rude, and it does not need a speech. A short, friendly answer, such as thanking the person and explaining that you cannot do it this time, is usually enough.
Maya learns a simple pattern for refusing: thank the person, say no clearly, and offer something small only if you want to. She practises it in the mirror until it sounds natural.
When a request surprises her, Maya has learned to say that she needs to check and will reply tomorrow. This small delay stops her agreeing in a panic and gives her time to think.
Saying no to bad ideas is easy, but the hardest refusals are for good ones. Maya is invited to join a lovely book club, and she turns it down to protect her painting evenings.
Dev asks her three times to take over his report, and each time he sounds a little more upset. Maya repeats her answer in the same calm voice, and in the end he finds another way.
After her first few refusals Maya feels guilty, as though she has done something wrong. She reminds herself that guilt is only a feeling, and by the evening it has faded.
Not every request needs a no, and Maya learns to give a yes with limits. She tells Ines that she can join the committee if it meets for no more than one hour a month.
Maya's friend Sam cancels their plans at the last minute almost every time. Maya feels hurt, but she has never told Sam, and so nothing has changed.
Maya says nothing about her hurt, but it comes out in other ways. She replies to Sam's messages coldly and a little late, and Sam cannot understand why.
A boundary is not a wall, and it is not a rule for somebody else. It simply says what you will do, and what you will not.
Before she meets Sam, Maya writes down what she wants to say. She plans to speak about her own feelings rather than to blame, and to ask for one clear change.
Maya decides to be honest and tells Sam that last-minute cancellations make her feel unimportant. Sam is surprised, apologises, and promises to tell her earlier next time.
Sam admits to saying yes to everyone and then being unable to keep all the promises. Maya realises, for the first time, that Sam is as overloaded as she has been.
Boundaries work in both directions, so they apply to you as well as to others. If you want others to accept your no, you must also accept theirs without sulking, arguing or making them feel guilty.
Maya has told Dev that she will answer messages only during work hours, but his late messages keep coming. Arguing again would waste her coins, so she simply mutes her phone at night.
Some of the most important boundaries are the ones we set with ourselves. Maya now charges her phone in the hallway at night, and her evenings and her sleep are calmer.
On Saturday Sam arrives at the cafe ten minutes early and waves from the door. The chair that used to be empty is full, and the friendship feels warmer than it has in years.

Maya scrolls through pictures of friends' holidays, promotions and perfect dinners, and she feels behind. There will always be someone with more, so the only fair comparison is with the person you were last year.
A friend from school posts that she has a new house and a new job. Maya is happy for her, but she also feels a sharp little pain that she did not expect.
What you see online is a shop window, arranged to look as good as possible. People post their best moments and keep their arguments, money worries and bad days in the storeroom at the back.
Maya finds a notebook from last year and reads her old worries. Most of them have disappeared, and she can see clearly how much she has grown since then.
Maya feels envious of a friend who writes books, and she wonders what the feeling is telling her. It tells her that she wants to write, so she asks whether she is ready to pay the price.
Leo watches a video of a fourteen-year-old who plays faster than he ever will. He feels so small that he puts his guitar down and does not touch it for two days.
Ms Okafor reminds Leo that nobody begins from the same starting line. The young star has played since the age of five, and he has far more free time than Leo.
Maya decides to celebrate her friend's success instead of measuring herself against it. She sends a warm message, and to her surprise the pain turns into real gladness.
Maya goes through the accounts she follows and asks which ones leave her feeling worse. She mutes twelve of them and keeps the ones that teach her something or make her laugh.
Maya starts a list in her notebook and gives it the title Better Than Last Year. It includes saying no, finishing things and sleeping well, and it is longer than she expected.
Billboards, videos and speeches all tell us that we are meant to be extraordinary. Beneath one such billboard a crowd of tired commuters hurries past, and each of them feels a little behind.
By definition, most people are average at most things, and this includes you and me. That is not a tragedy, because an ordinary life can still be rich, useful and full of meaning.
The belief that you must be special causes a lot of misery, because it makes ordinary days feel like failures. Pick one or two things to become good at, and enjoy the rest simply as part of living.
A great violinist may play beautifully and still burn the toast and get lost on the way home. Being excellent at one thing leaves a person ordinary at almost everything else.
On Saturday Maya makes soup, listens to the radio and phones her aunt for a chat. Nothing about the day is special, yet she goes to bed feeling content.
Leo asks Ms Okafor whether there is any point in playing if he will never be great. She laughs kindly and says that people sing in the shower without hoping for a record contract.
Accepting that you are ordinary does not mean that you should stop trying or stop caring. Maya still takes care to do her work well, simply because she likes doing things well.
Aunt Nora ran a small corner shop for thirty years, and she never became famous. When she closed it, half the street came to say goodbye, and many of them cried.
Once Maya stops pretending to be special, she finds it easier to ask simple questions. She asks the man at the hardware shop how a tap works, and he is delighted to explain.
For one week Maya does her painting and her walking without telling a soul or posting a single picture. She is surprised to find that she enjoys them just as much, and perhaps more.
A short complaint can feel like a relief, but a long one only keeps you stuck. Next time you start, stop and ask yourself what single step you could take to improve the situation.
When we complain, people nod and agree, and it feels as though we have done something. Afterwards the problem is exactly the same size as before, and we are a little more tired.
When Maya notices that she is complaining about her messy filing system, she asks what one step she could take. The answer is to spend fifteen minutes on Friday sorting one drawer.
Sometimes nothing can be done, as with bad weather, a long queue or a cancelled flight. Then it is fine to say that it is annoying, and then to let it go.
Every morning three colleagues gather by the coffee machine to complain about the company. Maya used to join in, but today she says that she has a call to make and walks away.
Instead of grumbling that the meetings are too early, Maya asks Ines whether they can start at ten. Ines considers it for a moment and agrees, which surprises everyone, including Maya.
Dev tells everyone that he is always unlucky, and that things simply happen to him. Maya notices that when she tells her own story as a person who makes choices, the same facts feel different.
Each night Maya writes down three small things that went well that day, such as a kind word or a warm shower. This does not hide her problems from her, but it puts them in proportion.
Leo spends a whole lesson complaining that scales are boring and pointless. Then Ms Okafor asks what he would like to play, and he sees that scales are the road to it.
Maya keeps a small card on her fridge that says, One step today. Whenever a complaint rises in her, she reads it and chooses one small step.
We are afraid of boredom, so we fill every quiet moment with a screen. If you leave a few gaps instead, you may notice what you actually think and what you actually enjoy.
In the supermarket queue Maya reaches for her phone, as she always does. This time she stops, puts it back in her pocket and simply looks around her.
On the train home Maya looks out of the window without her phone. After ten minutes of boredom the answer to a work problem arrives, and she writes it down.
Maya takes her usual walk without headphones for the first time in years. She hears birds, footsteps and a distant bell, and she realises how much she has been missing.
Maya used to rush through the washing-up while listening to the news. Tonight she does it slowly, feels the warm water, and discovers that a dull job can be a calm moment.
One weekend Maya decides to spend on pure pleasure, with pastries, films and a long shopping trip. By Sunday evening the fun has faded, and she feels strangely flat.

Pleasure is lovely, but it is quick to fade, and chasing it all the time never satisfies you for long. Meaning comes from giving your effort to something that matters, and it stays with you much longer.
Aunt Nora has a bad cold, so Maya spends her Sunday cooking a stew and carrying it across town. It is hard work, and it leaves her with a quiet warmth that lasts all week.
Raising children, caring for a parent or learning a hard skill is rarely relaxing. These things are tiring, yet many people who do them would never trade them for an easy life.
Maya asks herself which activities leave her tired in a good way, and which leave her only empty. The first list is short, and she decides to give it more of her week.
A grudge is like carrying a heavy stone to show someone how much they hurt you. Forgiving does not mean you approve of what they did, but it does let you put the stone down.
Three years ago a colleague named Rob presented Maya's idea as his own. She has never forgotten it, and she thinks about it far more often than he ever does.
In the shower, on the train and even at dinner, Maya imagines clever speeches that she will never give to Rob. Each speech wins the argument, and each one costs her a handful of coins.
Mr Haddad listens to Maya's story over tea and then tells her something simple. Forgiving a person does not mean saying that the wrong was acceptable, and it does not mean seeing them again.
Maya writes Rob a long, honest letter that says everything she has held back. She does not send it, yet writing it loosens something tight inside her.
Maya realises that she is still keeping a mental list of every time Sam let her down. She tears it up in her mind, because the new rule is working and the old list only keeps the hurt alive.
Last week Maya snapped at Dev in front of the team, and it has bothered her ever since. Today she goes to his desk and says that she is sorry.
A good apology says clearly what you did, says that you are sorry, and offers to put it right. It does not include the word but, because but cancels everything that came before it.
Maya still feels ashamed of a mistake that she made at twenty-two, when she let a friend down. She asks how she would treat a friend in the same situation, and she gives herself the same kindness.
With the old grudges put down, Maya notices that her days feel less crowded. She has more coins left at the end of each day, and she spends them on things she enjoys.
A local band needs a new guitarist, and Leo decides that he will audition. He practises two songs every evening for three weeks, even when his fingers ache.
Leo sits in the corridor with cold hands and a dry mouth, waiting for his name. Maya reminds him that nervousness is only a signal that this matters to him.
Leo plays his two songs for three musicians who sit behind a drum kit. His fingers tremble, he makes one clear mistake, and he finishes the last chord as well as he can.
Leo auditions for a local band and is turned down. He feels awful for a day, but then he asks the band what he could improve and starts working on exactly that.
Leo is quiet for most of the bus ride home, and Maya does not try to hurry him towards feeling better. She sits beside him, and that is exactly what he needs.
The drummer tells Leo three honest things: keep a steady beat, look up, and play fewer notes. Leo writes them down without arguing, even though one of them stings.
Maya explains to Leo that criticism comes in three kinds: useful advice, matters of taste, and unkind remarks. He should act on the first, think about the second and ignore the third.
Ines tells Maya that her report is clear but much too long, and Maya's face grows hot. She wants to defend every page, but she takes a slow breath and listens.
Maya reminds herself that a weak report is not the same as a weak person. The report can be cut in half and improved, but Maya herself does not need fixing.
A month later Leo plays two songs at a cafe's open evening, with a steady beat and his eyes up. Nobody offers him a contract, but a stranger tells him that she loved it.
In a cupboard Maya finds a ukulele, a pair of knitting needles and a Spanish grammar book. Each was exciting for about three weeks, and then it was quietly forgotten.
There is a freedom in saying that this is the thing I will do. People who try everything for a little while never reach the depth that comes from sticking with one path.
A person who keeps every door open never walks all the way through any of them. Options feel like freedom, but they cost attention every time you have to think about them.
Maya decides to pick one thing and give it a full season before she judges it. Seeds do not grow in a week, and neither does a skill.
To choose well, Maya reads her old lists of values, struggles and good tiredness. One thing appears on all three lists, and it is painting.
Maya promised to watch Leo play at his school concert. On the same evening she is invited to a glamorous party, but she keeps her promise and goes to the concert.
Commitment does not mean that you are never allowed to stop anything. Maya decides, on purpose, to give her ukulele to a charity shop, and she feels clear instead of guilty.
Dev has stayed on a dull evening course for months because he has already paid for it. Maya tells him that the money is gone either way, and the only question is what is best from now on.
Maya thinks carefully about leaving her job, and decides that it is worth keeping. She asks Ines for fewer projects and clearer hours, and Ines agrees to a trial.
Maya pays for a whole year of painting classes and writes it in her notebook as her one new pursuit. She feels a small tremor of fear, and then a larger wave of relief.
On her birthday Maya blows out the candles and feels a small shock that another year has gone. It does not make her sad, but it makes her curious about the next one.
Your time is limited, and nobody can tell you exactly how much of it remains. That sounds sad, but it is also what makes each choice about your attention important.
A person who lives to eighty will have about four thousand weeks in all. That sounds like a lot until you draw them as small squares on a long strip of paper.
In his flat Mr Haddad has shelves of old clocks, and every one of them shows a different time. He smiles and says that he could mend any clock, but never time itself.
Try to imagine yourself as a very old person looking back at your life. Which worries will seem silly, and which relationships and efforts will you be glad that you put first?
Maya asks Mr Haddad what he is most glad about, looking back over his life. He talks about the people he loved and the work he did carefully, and he does not mention a single thing that he owned.
It is not pleasant to think that life ends, but it can be very useful. Thinking about it gently makes small worries shrink and important things look much clearer.
Maya climbs a hill outside the city and looks down at the roofs and the cars. From up there the awkward email that worried her yesterday seems as small as the traffic.
Maya has been meaning to phone her old school friend for three years. This evening she stops waiting for a perfect moment and dials the number.
Time is spent one day at a time, so Maya stops thinking only about the whole of life. She writes one meaningful thing in her notebook for the week ahead, and she does it on Tuesday.
A list with forty priorities is not a list but a pile. When everything is marked important, nothing is, and the person holding the pile cannot move.
To choose her five, Maya looks at three things: her values, the struggles she accepts and the people she loves. Anything that appears in two or more of them goes on the list.
Maya lists the five things she cares about most: her health, her family, her friends, one skill and her honesty. She pins it above her desk and agrees to say no to most of the rest.
When a new request arrives, Maya looks up at the card and asks whether it serves one of her five lines. Decisions that once took an hour now take about a minute.
Once a week, perhaps on Sunday morning, look at your calendar and ask where your coins really went. If the answer does not match your list, make one small change for the week ahead.
Maya's Sunday review has three questions, which are where her coins went, what gave her energy, and what she will change. She answers each one in a single short line and then closes the notebook.
You will forget all of this on some days, and you will find yourself worrying about everything again. That is normal, so simply notice it, smile, and go back to your list.
A very busy month arrives at work, and Maya cannot give all five lines their usual time. Instead of throwing the card away, she shrinks two lines for a month and notes when they will grow again.
Maya notices that on days when she sleeps badly and skips meals, her coins disappear faster. Sleep, simple food and a daily walk do not feel exciting, but they keep her bag full.
Dev notices that Maya is calmer, and he asks how she does it. She does not give a speech, but she shows him her card with its five short lines.
One morning Maya notices that every line on her card begins with the word my. Her card is a good one, but she feels that something larger is missing.
The best place for your coins is often something bigger than you, such as family, a neighbourhood or a cause. Such things give you a reason to continue when you are tired.
Maya joins the community garden for one hour every Saturday. The work is simple and muddy, and she soon knows the names of eleven neighbours she had never met.
Leo agrees to teach a small boy from the next street his first chord. Explaining it helps Leo understand his own playing more deeply, and the boy's joy is a bonus.

The news is full of problems that Maya cannot solve, and caring about all of them makes her feel helpless. She chooses one action within her reach, such as giving time to the garden, and lets the rest go.

Let us gather the main ideas together before we say goodbye. Choose your struggles, pick values you can live by, own your response, test your beliefs, say no kindly and compare yourself with your past.
Dev tries to write his own card, but he keeps adding lines and says that he is failing already. Maya tells him that this is a practice, not a switch, and that she still forgets her own.
Maya writes a short letter to herself and seals it in an envelope to open in one year. In it she writes what she has learned, and a promise to keep choosing.
On a quiet morning Maya sits at the same kitchen table where she once counted her coins. The bag is no bigger than before, but she now knows what she wants to buy with it.
Maya still has the same job and the same small bag of coins, but she spends them differently now. She cares about fewer things, and she cares about them much more.
C1C2: Every morning you are handed a small purse of coins, and you cannot refill it by wishing. The coins are your attention, your energy and your time, and every thought, worry or ambition quietly takes a few of them away. This book is about one skill that sounds simple and is surprisingly hard, which is deciding where those coins should go.

It is easy to forget that caring has a price, because the bill arrives slowly, as tiredness and distraction rather than as money. Each person, project and opinion that you care about takes a share of the same small supply. When the list grows too long, there is simply not enough left for the things that deserve it most.

Many of us live as though the supply of caring were endless, and we try to be admired at work, adored at home, fit, informed and wealthy all at the same time. The effort is admirable, but it leaves us thin, like a thin coat of paint over a very large wall. By evening we are tired without being able to say what we have actually achieved.

Maya works in a busy office, and she is the kind of person who answers every email within minutes and reads every headline before breakfast. She also wonders, constantly, what her colleagues think of her haircut, her ideas and her lunch. By Friday she is so drained that she spends the weekend on the sofa, wondering where her energy went.

Maya takes a sheet of paper and records, hour by hour, everything that held her attention during a single ordinary Tuesday. The list runs to two pages and includes forty minutes on a stranger's argument about parking, in which she had no part at all. She stares at it and realises that she has been spending her richest coins on the cheapest things.

Her colleague Dev thinks aloud in writing, and a new message from him arrives every few minutes, usually with a small question attached. Maya, who cannot bear to leave a message unanswered, drops whatever she is doing to reply, and so her own work is chopped into crumbs. By the afternoon she has been wonderfully helpful to everyone except the one person who needs her most, which is herself.

By the time Maya reaches her sofa, her mind feels like a purse that has been turned inside out and shaken. She has been busy for twelve hours, yet when she tries to list what she accomplished, the page stays almost blank. Being occupied and being effective, she is beginning to see, are two entirely different conditions.

It is important to say at once that this is not a book about becoming indifferent. Someone who feels nothing about anything is not free, only numb, and numbness is a poor way to live. The aim is the opposite, which is to care deeply and deliberately about a small number of things and to let the rest pass by.

Human beings cannot switch off caring, any more than they can switch off hunger. Something will always claim your attention, whether you chose it deliberately or it simply arrived while you were not looking. The only real question is whether you will pick the things that get your coins or leave the choice to advertisements, habits and other people's moods.

Maya is not a dramatic person, and she does not announce a revolution to anyone, but that night she buys a plain notebook and writes a single sentence on its first page. The sentence says that she will no longer let her attention be spent by whoever shouts loudest, and that she will choose where it goes. What follows is what she learns while keeping that promise, one awkward experiment at a time.

Maya's young cousin Leo dreams of playing the guitar on a stage, with lights above him and a crowd singing along. He is much less excited by the sore fingertips, the dull scales and the bad evenings that must come before that moment. Nobody ever receives the applause without first having paid for it, slowly and often alone, with hours of patient and unglamorous practice.

Every worthwhile goal arrives with its own particular kind of pain, and there is no route that avoids discomfort altogether. The athlete accepts aching muscles, the writer accepts empty pages and the parent accepts broken nights. The wise question is therefore which struggle you are willing to choose, because you will have one either way.

Where the park divides, one path runs flat and smooth beside the pond, while the other climbs steeply through loose stones to a high bench. Nothing is wrong with the easy path, and on some days it is exactly the right choice, but it will never show you what the hill can. Every kind of life offers such a pair of paths, and the useful question is which kind of effort you would rather spend.

Almost everyone wants a pleasant life, a rewarding job and a loving family, so wanting tells us very little about a person. What separates people is the discomfort they are willing to tolerate for what they want. Ask yourself, honestly, which kind of difficulty you could live with for years without resenting it.

Plenty of people announce that they want to learn a language, run a marathon or finish a novel. When they will not accept the dull, repetitive work that each of these demands, the wish is really a daydream wearing the clothes of a goal. Wanting the result, in other words, is cheap, while wanting the process is rare.

After a week of daily practice Leo's fingertips are sore, red and shiny, and he secretly decides that the guitar was a bad idea. His teacher, Ms Okafor, smiles when he shows her and explains that every guitarist has paid this exact bill, and that the skin soon grows tough. The pain, she says, is not a sign that he is doing it wrong but the first instalment on something he wants.

For three years Maya has told everyone that she wants to be fit, and the running shoes by her door look very hopeful. What she has never admitted is that she does not want the cold mornings, the burning lungs or the first slow weeks in which she will be bad at it. She loves the picture of the goal, but she has not yet agreed to the price, and that is why the shoes are still clean.

Dev has been offered a promotion, and he can already see the bigger salary and the better title shining at the end of the month. What he has not yet counted are the longer hours, the heavier responsibility and the dinners at home that will quietly disappear from his week. Every prize arrives with a bill attached, and a wise person reads the bill before deciding that the prize is worth having.

Notice that the baker in the corner shop laughs when a tray of loaves comes out of the oven dark and bitter, and that she simply tries again the next morning. The struggle is real, but it does not feel like a punishment, because it belongs to something she has chosen and loves. The best struggles are those that you would be a little sad to lose, since they are inseparable from the life you want.

In her notebook Maya writes a heading, Struggles I Accept, and beneath it she lists three items: early morning walks, difficult conversations with friends, and the dull parts of her work. She hesitates before each one, because each is an honest promise of discomfort, and then she signs the page like a tiny contract. It is the first list she has ever written that was not about what she wanted, but about what she was willing to pay.

A feeling is a message from your mind, and like any message it can be useful, mistaken or simply loud. Fear, envy and sadness belong to an ordinary human life, and their arrival does not prove that you are failing. You are allowed to listen to a feeling politely, to thank it for the warning, and still decide for yourself what to do next.

Ten minutes before an important presentation, Maya feels her heart pounding and her palms turning damp, and a loud inner voice insists that she should invent an excuse and leave. She treats the feeling as a command, as though the sensation itself proved that something terrible lay ahead. It is really a signal about what matters to her, however, and signals are meant to be read rather than obeyed.

Maya feels a little nervous before an important meeting, and then she becomes annoyed with herself for being nervous in the first place. That annoyance makes her anxious about being anxious, and soon she is carrying three heavy feelings where there was originally only one light one. The second layer of suffering, the distress about the distress, is very often far heavier than the first one ever was.

One grey afternoon Maya becomes convinced that her career is a failure, her flat is too small and her future is doomed. Then she remembers that she has skipped lunch, eats a sandwich and drinks a glass of water, and the whole landscape softens within the hour. Before you trust a very dark thought, it is worth asking whether you are simply tired, hungry or short of sleep.

There is another way, which is to say plainly that you feel nervous and to let the feeling sit beside you without arguing with it. Emotions that are not resisted tend to rise, reach a peak and gradually fade, much like waves on a beach. Fighting them is what keeps them alive, because every struggle feeds them fresh attention.

Maya tries a small experiment and, instead of sinking into the feeling, she names it quietly, telling herself that this is nervousness and that it has come because the presentation matters to her. The act of naming puts a little distance between her and the sensation, as if she were looking at a cloud instead of standing inside it. A clear word may not remove the weather, but it does turn a vague dread into something that can be understood.

At noon Maya was certain that the dread in her stomach would never leave, yet by four o'clock it has faded so far that she can hardly remember its shape. Feelings behave more like weather than like buildings, since they arrive, linger and move on without any permission from us. Knowing this will not make a hard hour pleasant, but it makes it far easier to survive without doing anything rash.

A curt email from a client makes Maya furious, and her fingers are already racing across the keyboard to compose a devastating reply. Then she remembers that a feeling is a signal rather than an order, and she closes the laptop and goes for a walk. The next morning her answer is calm, brief and fair, and she is quietly grateful to the woman who waited.

Pleasant feelings can mislead us just as easily as unpleasant ones, and perhaps more dangerously, because we never think to question them. Maya feels a glorious surge of excitement in a shop, buys a jacket that costs a week of her pay, and by the weekend it hangs in her wardrobe like a stranger. A feeling, whether it is joyful or gloomy, is a piece of information, and it should be weighed before it is obeyed.

Maya turns her new understanding into a small habit of three questions, which are what she is feeling, what it is trying to tell her, and what she wants to do about it. The questions take less than a minute, and they place a little space between the feeling and the action, which is exactly where choice lives. A low mood that lasts for weeks is different, and in that case the wise step is to talk to a doctor or someone you trust.

Your values are the yardsticks by which you judge whether you are succeeding, and everyone has them, whether or not they have ever put them into words. Some of these yardsticks are poorly chosen, for instance the need to be admired by everyone or to own more than the people next door. They fail because they depend on other people, and other people will never stay still long enough to satisfy you.

Dev lives by an unwritten rule that he must always be right, and he will defend even a trivial opinion about the best route to work as though his honour depended on it. He wins a great many arguments, and every victory costs him a little warmth, until his colleagues stop asking for his view at all. A value that can only be satisfied by making other people smaller is a poor one to build a life on.

Maya spreads her calendar and her bank statement across the table and asks what a stranger would conclude about her values from them alone. The stranger would say that she values speed, approval and constant availability, which is not at all the answer she would have given if anyone had asked. Our real values are written less in our speeches than in our habits, and they are surprisingly easy to read once we look.

Healthier values are those that you can express entirely through your own behaviour, such as honesty, curiosity, generosity and perseverance. No critic can cancel them and no market can crash them, and they remain available on your very worst days. A life measured by such standards is steadier because success lies in your own hands.

Mr Haddad, an elderly neighbour who spent most of his life repairing other people's clocks, is struggling up the steps with two heavy bags of shopping. Maya takes them without being asked, and as they climb together she realises that no one is watching, no one will reward her, and she feels more like herself than she has all week. This is what living by a value feels like, since it is quiet and immediate and is its own payment.

Here is a practical test for any value you are considering, which is whether you could act on it this very afternoon, even if nobody noticed and nobody helped you. Being honest passes the test easily, since you can do it in the next five minutes, whereas becoming famous fails it at once. Choose standards that pass, and you will always have something real to work towards, however the rest of the day turns out.

Leo has always measured himself against an imaginary crowd, and it has made every living-room performance feel like a rehearsal for something bigger. Being famous cannot be done this afternoon, whereas playing as well as he can for whoever is in the room can be done at once. He tries it for his mother and for Maya, and the little room feels, for the first time, like the right size for music.

To discover her values, Maya recalls the three days of the past year when she felt most fully herself, and she searches them for a common thread. One was spent helping a friend move house, one was spent finishing a stubborn report, and one was spent telling a difficult truth kindly. The thread, she sees, is that she feels best when she is useful, careful and honest, and that is a better compass than any slogan.

Maya writes three words on a small card, which are honest, useful and curious, and she props it against the lamp beside her bed. She does not imagine that these words will stay exactly the same for ever, since values mature as a person does, but they will do for now. A good value is not a decoration to be admired but a tool that she will pick up many times a day.

A goal is a place on the map, and once you arrive you can cross it off and enjoy the small thrill of finishing. A value is more like a direction, such as north, which you can follow all your life without ever arriving. This is why values make a steadier foundation than goals alone, since there is always one more step you can take towards them today.

Take a sheet of paper and draw two circles, one for the things you can truly control and one for everything else. Your effort, your words and your next small action belong in the first circle, whereas the weather, the economy and other people's opinions belong firmly in the second. Most of our worry is spent on the second circle, where it can accomplish nothing at all.

Maya fills in her two circles as honestly as she can, and the result is a little humbling. Her sleep, her replies and the effort she puts into the next hour fit into the small circle, while the traffic, her manager's mood, the news and what Sam might think of her crowd into the huge one outside. Seeing the drawing, she understands why she is tired, since most of her worry has been spent where nothing can be done.

Events arrive uninvited, and no amount of planning can prevent every delay, illness or disappointment. What remains yours, however, is the response, meaning the attitude you adopt, the action you take and the story you tell yourself afterwards. Spending your coins on the response rather than on the event is one of the best bargains available.

On Monday the morning train is forty minutes late, and the crowd on the platform seethes with sighs and glares at the departure board. Maya notices that every glare is aimed at something nobody present can change, and she quietly opens the book in her bag instead. The delay is outside her control, but what she makes of the next forty minutes is entirely her own.

When Maya passes two colleagues whispering by the coffee machine, her mind instantly constructs an entire conversation about her flaws. She has to remind herself that what other people think is the weather of their own minds, which she can influence a little through her conduct but can never command. What she can do is behave well, speak honestly and let the opinions fall where they may.

Maya cannot decide whether her audience will applaud or yawn, and she cannot decide whether Ines will like her proposal. What she can decide is how carefully she prepares, so she practises the talk twice in an empty meeting room and trims two weak slides. To judge herself by her effort rather than by the reaction is a relief, because effort is the only part of the whole affair that belongs to her.

Imagine that a storm throws your neighbour's tree across your garden fence, so that the fault is plainly nobody's and certainly not yours. The fence is nevertheless your concern, since you are the one who will have to look at the gap, and the damage will not repair itself. Fault looks backwards at who caused a problem, whereas responsibility looks forwards at who will deal with it.

A glass slips from a tray in the office kitchen and shatters across the floor, and the fault belongs to a colleague who has already hurried away. Maya could stand there composing a complaint, but the glittering fragments are still a danger to bare feet, and she is the one who has noticed them. She fetches the broom, and the small decision feels strangely powerful, as if she had bought back a little of her own day.

Blame is tempting because it feels like justice, and it spares us the effort of doing anything difficult. Unfortunately, it also hands control of our lives to the very people we blame, since we are now waiting for them to put things right. Once you accept responsibility, even for a mess you did not make, you become the person who can finally begin to fix it.

Sam sends yet another message to say that dinner is cancelled, and Maya feels a flash of irritation that she has not earned. The habit is Sam's and not Maya's fault, but how she responds to it is her responsibility, and she could respond by sulking, by staying silent or by being honest. She decides to use the next few days to choose carefully, because that part she can control, even if she cannot control Sam.

Certainty is comfortable in the way that an old armchair is comfortable, because it asks nothing of us and lets us stop thinking. Yet every one of us carries a few firm beliefs that are wrong, and the cruel part is that they feel exactly as true as the ones that are right. Wisdom begins with the humble suspicion that some of your most comfortable certainties are, in fact, quietly and stubbornly mistaken.

Leo has always insisted that he is hopeless at maths, and he says it with the confidence of a man reporting the weather. When Maya gently asks what would follow if he were mistaken, he thinks for a moment and admits that nobody ever explained fractions to him in a way that made sense. A belief that has never been tested is only a habit with good manners.

For as long as she can remember, Maya has announced that she is simply not a creative person, and she says it with the calm of someone stating her height. When she finally asks where the belief came from, she traces it to a single careless remark by a school teacher, made when she was eleven. A belief that has been repeated for twenty years can feel like a fact, but its age proves only how often it has been repeated.

Maya adopts a small and slightly uncomfortable habit, which is to ask herself, whenever she feels completely certain, what she would see if she were wrong. The question does not oblige her to change her mind, but it forces her to look at the evidence she has been politely ignoring. Within a week it has saved her from two pointless arguments and from one embarrassing email.

You do not need to abandon a belief in one dramatic moment, and nobody is asking you to. Choose one that you suspect is false, behave as though the opposite were true for a month, and write down honestly what happens. Evidence gathered from your own life is far more convincing than any argument, however clever.

Maya invites Dev to lunch and asks him to explain, as fairly as he can, why he disagrees with her about how the team should work. She listens without preparing her reply, which is harder than it sounds, and she discovers that his view rests on two facts she had never considered. She does not abandon her opinion, but it becomes narrower, kinder and a good deal more accurate.

Most of us hold firm opinions about foreign countries, diets, economics and the private lives of strangers, though we have studied none of them in any depth. Often the whole opinion rests on a headline glimpsed on a phone, or on something a confident friend once said at dinner. The more strongly you feel about a subject, the more it is worth asking how much of it you have actually looked into.

In a meeting Maya is asked a technical question that she cannot answer, and for a second she feels the old urge to bluff her way through. Instead she says plainly that she does not know and that she will find out by Friday, and the room does not collapse. Ines nods with something like respect, because people trust those who can say where their knowledge ends.

Maya used to feel that changing her mind was a kind of surrender, and she would defend a position long after she had stopped believing in it. Now she regards it as evidence that she is still alive to new information, and she can even say with a smile that she was wrong. The people who cannot do this risk becoming more rigid with the years, while those who can have a chance of growing wiser.

For a month Maya tests her old belief by drawing something small, a mug or a shoe or a plant, for ten minutes every evening. The first drawings are clumsy, but by the end of the month the pile of pages shows a clear, if modest, improvement that no argument could have produced. She cannot honestly go on calling herself uncreative, and she feels a little sad for the years she spent believing it.

No child has ever learned to ride a bicycle without wobbling, falling and getting up again with a scraped knee. We accept this calmly for children, yet as adults we expect ourselves to succeed at the first attempt and are devastated when we do not. Failure is not the opposite of learning but one of its most necessary and most honest stages, and it deserves a little respect.

Ms Okafor takes out her old practice notebook from her student days, and Leo is astonished to find it full of crossed-out lines, tired scribbles and furious little notes to herself. She explains that every expert he admires was once a beginner who got things wrong many times before the music finally behaved. What looks like talent from a distance is, on closer inspection, mostly a very large pile of survived mistakes.

On Thursday evening Maya stands outside a small door with a hand-lettered sign that reads Evening Painting Class, her coat still buttoned to the chin. She can hear voices and gentle laughter inside, and her nervousness is far greater than it was before her presentation. Everything in her wants to walk quietly back to the station and tell herself that she was too busy.

Maya has wanted to join a painting class for years, but she is terrified that she might turn out to be bad at it in front of strangers. Then she changes the definition of success from producing a masterpiece to turning up and learning something new. With that single adjustment the fear loses most of its grip, because she can no longer lose.

The teacher, Mr Lam, asks the whole class to paint a single apple in forty minutes, and Maya's turns out lumpy, lopsided and distinctly potato-like. She waits for the wave of shame that she has dreaded for years, but what arrives instead is a laugh, which spreads quietly to the person beside her. She has failed in public, and nothing has happened to her, except that she has had a very good evening.

At a family dinner Leo reaches the difficult chord in the middle of his song and plays it badly, and his face turns the colour of a tomato. For a moment he considers stopping, but he takes a breath, finds the right fingers and carries on, and the room continues to hum along as though nothing had happened. By dessert nobody remembers the slip except Leo, who is learning that mistakes are far more private than they feel.

When we make a mistake in public, it feels as though a spotlight has been switched on and everyone is staring at us. In reality most of the people around us are occupied with their own faces, their own worries and their own mistakes, and they forget our slips within minutes. The audience that judges you hardest, and for longest, is almost always the one inside your own head.

When something goes badly, Maya no longer replays it over and over in the dark of the night. She writes down what happened, what it taught her and what she will try differently next time, and then she closes the notebook and lets the matter rest. A mistake that has been examined is a lesson, whereas a mistake that has only been regretted is merely a weight.

Maya notices that she is much braver when the price of failure is low, so she begins to collect small experiments, such as a new recipe, a different route home or a sketch in a cafe. A burnt dinner costs only a little money and a little pride, and it teaches her something every single time. Courage, she concludes, is easier to build with many cheap failures than with one expensive leap.

At the end of the course Mr Lam studies Maya's painting of the river for a long minute, and then he points to a single bright corner. He tells her that this is the part where she stopped trying to be correct and simply looked, and that it is the best part of the picture. Maya takes it home, pins it above her kitchen table, and realises that she has not once thought about failing since the first evening.

Most of us believe that motivation must come first and action second, and so we sit and wait for the mood to arrive. In practice the order is often reversed, since a small, almost laughable first step produces the energy needed for the second. Begin badly if you have to, because momentum can only be built from something that has started.

When a task seems enormous, make yourself a very small promise, which is to work on it for five minutes and then stop if you wish. The trick is that beginning is nearly always the hardest part, and once you are inside the work it tends to carry you along. Even on the days when it does not, five minutes is still five minutes more than you had before.

Maya's grand plan to get fit, learn to paint and reorganise her entire flat feels thrilling for exactly one evening. By the following morning the plan has swollen into something so huge and shapeless that she cannot find a place to begin, and so she begins nothing. Large plans stall not because we are lazy but because the first step is hidden somewhere inside the fog of the whole.

Maya shrinks every first step until it is almost laughable: one stretch instead of a workout, one sentence instead of a chapter, one minute of tidying instead of an afternoon. These tiny tasks are so easy that her mind can find no sensible excuse to refuse them, and so she does them. Once the first step is taken, a surprising number of the second ones follow without any argument.

Maya discovers that a new habit survives much better when it is fastened to an old one, so she ties her notebook to the first cup of tea in the morning. While the kettle slowly rumbles to the boil, she writes one honest line about the day ahead, and the old habit pulls the new one along behind it. The kettle, which was once just a kettle, has become a small daily reminder of who she is trying to be.

On the days when she comes home drained and defeated, Maya refuses to abandon her habits and instead does the smallest possible version of each. One line in the notebook, one stretch or one minute at the easel will do, because the aim on such days is not progress but survival. A habit that is kept alive through a bad week will flower again, whereas a habit that is dropped must be rebuilt from nothing.

Leo comes home from school with heavy eyes, and the thought of a full hour of scales feels like a mountain. He makes himself a bargain of ten minutes only, with permission to stop the moment the little clock rings. When it does ring, his fingers have warmed and his mind has woken up, and he plays on for twenty minutes more simply because he wants to.

Leo takes his guitar out of its case and sets it on a stand in the middle of the room, while Maya lays out her shoes by the door the night before. Both of them have discovered that a habit depends less on willpower than on how much friction lies between you and the first step. Remove a few small obstacles, and the thing you want to do becomes the thing that is easiest to do.

Maya hangs a plain calendar beside her door and marks a small blue cross on every day that she keeps her habit, however modest the effort has been. The row of crosses lengthens, and the sight of it gives her a quiet satisfaction that no inspirational speech has ever provided. Progress that is invisible is easy to doubt, but progress that can be counted on a wall is very hard to argue with.

After two weeks Maya turns back to the first page of her sketchbook and compares it with the most recent one. Nothing dramatic has occurred, and no single day felt important, yet the difference is as plain as the difference between a seed and a seedling. Real progress, she sees, is usually quiet, and it arrives in the shape of many small things repeated until they add up to something large.

Every yes quietly contains a no, because the hours you give to one thing can never be spent on another. Agreeing to every invitation, favour and committee therefore means refusing your own priorities again and again without ever noticing. Those who guard their time are not selfish, only honest about how little of it there is.

Maya pictures a corridor with two doors, one labelled yes and one labelled no, and she realises that for years she has walked through the first without even glancing at the second. Each time she did so, something behind the other door, such as an evening of painting or a quiet night's sleep, was quietly left behind. A yes that is given without any thought is not really generosity, but a kind of drifting.

In a single week Maya agrees to help Dev with his report, to join a committee for Ines, to mind a neighbour's cat and to attend two birthday drinks that she does not want to attend. When she looks at her calendar on Sunday, it is crammed from corner to corner, and not one entry belongs to her. She has been generous with everyone except her own life, and the bill is beginning to arrive.

A refusal does not have to be cold, and it does not need a long and nervous list of excuses. Thank the person, say plainly that you cannot take it on this time, and stop talking before you start apologising. Most people respect a clear no far more than a vague yes that is later broken.

Maya learns a pattern for refusing that has three parts, which are to thank the person sincerely, to say no clearly, and to offer something small only if she really wants to. She practises it aloud in the bathroom mirror until the words stop sounding like a confession and begin to sound like a plain fact. The shorter the refusal is, she finds, the more kindly and easily it is received by others.

When a request catches her by surprise, Maya has learned to say that she needs to check her plans and will reply tomorrow. This small delay rescues her from the old reflex of agreeing in a panic, and it gives her time to weigh the request against the coins she has left. Most people, she finds, are perfectly content to wait for an answer that is considered rather than one that is instant.

Refusing a bad idea is easy, and the really difficult refusals are for opportunities that are perfectly good. Maya is invited to join a lively book club, which she would enjoy, and she declines it so that her Thursday evenings stay free for painting. The choice stings a little, but it is what it means to have priorities, since a priority that never costs you anything is only a wish.

Dev asks Maya three times to take over his report, and each time his arguments grow a little more ingenious and his voice a little more wounded. She does not raise her voice, offer new excuses or apologise, but repeats her answer kindly in the same words, like a patient clock. In the end he sighs, shrugs and finds another way, and she discovers that a calm no is much sturdier than she had feared.

After her first firm refusals Maya is troubled by waves of guilt, as though she had stolen something rather than simply protected her time. She recalls what she has learned about feelings, which is that they are signals and not orders, and she lets this one pass. By the evening it has faded to a faint bruise, and by the next week it has gone altogether.

Not every request deserves a flat refusal, and Maya discovers a third answer, which is a yes with conditions. She tells Ines that she will happily join the committee if it meets for no longer than one hour a month, and she is delighted when the offer is accepted. A clear limit, spoken at the beginning, spares everybody the later disappointment of a promise that was too large to keep.

Maya's friend Sam has a habit of cancelling their plans at the last possible moment, and each time Maya says it is fine while feeling quietly hurt. She has never told Sam how she feels, so Sam has no way of knowing that anything is wrong. A limit that is never spoken aloud is only a resentment waiting for a convenient time to appear.

Maya says nothing about her hurt, but unspoken feelings are rarely content to stay quiet. They leak out in cooler replies, in slower answers and in a certain sharpness in her voice, and Sam, who has no idea what has changed, grows puzzled and then defensive. Silence has not protected the friendship, only allowed a small injury to turn into a larger and stranger one.

A boundary is sometimes imagined as a wall built against other people, but it is closer to a garden gate, which tells visitors where to come in. It is not a rule that you impose on somebody else's behaviour, since you cannot control that, but a plain statement about what you will and will not do. Understood in this way, a boundary is not a punishment but a piece of honest information that helps people treat you well.

Before she meets Sam, Maya writes down exactly what she wants to say, and she deletes every sentence that sounds like an accusation. She plans instead to describe how the cancellations make her feel, to say what she needs, and to ask for one clear change. Honest words are most easily heard when they describe your own experience, because nobody can argue with how you feel.

Eventually Maya finds the courage to tell Sam that last-minute cancellations make her feel unimportant, and she says it calmly rather than angrily. Sam is surprised, then apologetic, and the two of them agree on a simple rule about giving notice. The conversation was uncomfortable for about ten minutes, yet it improved the friendship for years and spared them both a great deal of silent resentment.

Sam listens, and then Sam confesses, with some embarrassment, to saying yes to everybody and then being unable to keep all the promises. Maya hears, for the first time, that the cancellations were never about her, but about a person who was stretched far thinner than she had imagined. Understanding the reason does not remove the need for a boundary, yet it changes the tone in which it can be spoken.

Limits are a two-way street, and it would be unfair to demand respect for yours while trampling on those of other people. When a friend says no, accept it without sulking, bargaining or making them feel guilty for having said it. Relationships grow stronger when both people can speak honestly and nobody has to fear the answer.

Maya has told Dev kindly that she will answer messages during working hours only, but his late-night questions keep arriving as though she had said nothing. She does not argue a second time, because a boundary is kept by actions and not by speeches, and so she simply mutes her phone after nine and answers him in the morning. After a week the late messages quietly thin out, and nothing terrible has happened to anyone.

Some of the most important boundaries are not set with other people at all but with ourselves, since we are often the ones who break them. Maya starts charging her phone in the hallway overnight, which removes the temptation to scroll until her eyes ache, and her sleep and her mornings begin to improve. It is a very small rule, yet it protects a surprisingly large number of her coins each night.

On Saturday Sam walks into the cafe ten minutes early and waves from the doorway, slightly breathless and clearly pleased with the achievement. The chair that was so often empty is occupied at last, and the friendship feels warmer, easier and more honest than it has in years. A boundary, Maya reflects over the coffee, did not push Sam away but gave the two of them a place to meet.

Late at night Maya scrolls through photographs of other people's holidays, promotions and immaculate dinners, and she concludes that everyone else is winning. There will always be somebody richer, stronger or luckier, so the contest is endless and impossible to win. The only comparison worth making is with the person you were a year ago.

A friend from school posts a bright announcement of a new house, a new job and a new puppy, and Maya clicks a smiling face before she has finished reading. She is truly happy for her friend, but beneath the happiness there is a small sharp pain that she did not expect and does not like. Feelings of this kind are not wicked, merely human, and the useful thing is to notice them without being ruled by them.

What you see on a screen is a shop window, carefully arranged to look as appealing as possible. People post their holidays and their triumphs, while their arguments, money worries and sleepless nights stay in the storeroom at the back, where no camera ever goes. Comparing your whole untidy life with someone else's polished highlights is a contest you are bound to lose.

Maya finds an old diary from last spring in a drawer and reads it with a mixture of embarrassment and tenderness. The worries that filled its pages, about a job, a cough and a quarrel, have mostly dissolved, and the person writing them seems younger and a good deal more frightened than she is today. Measured against the strangers on her phone she is always behind, but measured against that earlier woman she is plainly ahead.

When Maya feels a pang of envy towards a friend who has just published a small book of poems, she resists the urge to be ashamed and asks what the feeling is trying to tell her. The answer is that she, too, would like to write, which is useful news indeed. Envy is a wasteful habit when it is merely suffered, but it becomes a useful compass when it is questioned honestly and linked to the price of the thing.

Leo watches a video of a fourteen-year-old guitarist whose fingers fly across the strings with astonishing speed, and a cold weight settles in his stomach. He puts his own guitar down and does not touch it for two days, convinced that his small progress has been a joke. Comparing his first year of practice with somebody else's tenth is a game that he is certain to lose, but he does not yet see that.

Ms Okafor reminds Leo that a race can only be compared fairly when everyone begins from the same line, and life never arranges things so neatly. The young guitarist has played since the age of five, has instruments and teachers in his house, and has hours of free time that Leo does not. The sensible response is not to resent such differences but to run your own race at your own pace, with your own head down.

Maya decides to celebrate her friend's success rather than use it as a ruler against her own, and so she writes a long and warm message of congratulation. She had expected it to be an act of politeness, but halfway through she finds that the sharp little pain has changed into real gladness. Another person's good fortune, she begins to see, is not a slice taken out of her own.

Maya goes through the accounts that she follows and asks of each one a plain question, which is whether it leaves her feeling better or worse. She mutes a dozen of them without any drama, and she keeps the ones that teach her something, show her something beautiful or simply make her laugh. What we allow into our attention shapes what we care about, and she has decided to be the editor of her own feed.

Maya starts a new list in her notebook and gives it the title Better Than Last Year, expecting to write two or three lines and to feel foolish. She fills most of a page, including saying no, finishing what she starts, speaking up in meetings and sleeping through the night more often than not. The comparison that once made her feel behind has become the one that shows her, quietly and fairly, how far she has come.

Billboards, videos and graduation speeches all repeat the same message, which is that you are meant to be extraordinary. Beneath one such billboard a crowd of tired commuters hurries to work, and each of them is privately wondering why they have not yet become the special person promised. A promise that cannot be kept for most of the people who hear it is a strange foundation for a happy life.

By definition, most people are fairly average at most of what they do, and the same is true of you and of me. This is not a tragedy, because an ordinary life can still be warm, useful and full of meaning. The pressure to be exceptional at everything is a modern invention, and you are free to put it down.

The belief that you must be extraordinary causes a surprising amount of misery, because it turns every ordinary day into a small disappointment.
