It is wiser to choose one or two pursuits in which you would like to grow and to enjoy everything else simply as part of being alive. A good conversation and a warm meal are not consolation prizes but the substance of a decent life.

A gifted violinist may play so beautifully that audiences weep, and yet she may burn the toast, forget birthdays and take a wrong turn on the way home. Excellence in one narrow field leaves a person entirely ordinary in nearly every other, and the same is true of the most celebrated people you can name. If the exceptional are mostly ordinary, then ordinariness cannot be the failure that we have been taught to fear.

On Saturday Maya makes a pot of soup, listens to an old radio programme and telephones her aunt for no reason except to chat. Nothing about the day would impress a stranger, and she posts no picture of it, yet she goes to bed with a deep and solid feeling of contentment. Small pleasures are not consolation prizes for people who failed to become special, but the very material from which most happy days are made.

Leo asks Ms Okafor, rather gloomily, whether there is any point in playing if he is never going to be great. She laughs kindly and points out that people sing in the shower, hum in the kitchen and dance at weddings without any hope of a record contract. Music, she says, belongs to everyone who enjoys it, and enjoying it is a perfectly good reason to keep going.

Accepting that you are ordinary does not mean giving up on good work, and it does not turn effort into a waste of time. Maya still mends the torn cover of an old book carefully, and she still checks every number in her reports, because she enjoys the quiet pride of a small job well done. Craft is available to everybody, and it asks only for attention, not for greatness.

Aunt Nora ran a small corner shop for thirty years, and she never appeared in a newspaper, a film or a list of the most successful people of her decade. On the day she locked the door for the last time, half the street came to say goodbye, and several of them wept openly. Maya, standing in the small crowd, thinks that few lives are more successful than one that has been so quietly useful.

Once Maya stops trying to appear exceptional, she finds it much easier to ask simple questions and to admit what she has not yet learned. She asks the man in the hardware shop how a leaking tap works, and he is so pleased to be asked that he explains it for twenty minutes. Without the burden of looking clever, she is free to be curious, and curiosity turns out to be much more enjoyable than pretending.

For one week Maya paints, walks and reads without telling a soul or posting a single picture of any of it. She had half expected the pleasure to shrink without an audience, but it grows richer instead, because nothing is being performed. A life that is lived for its own sake, she begins to suspect, is lighter to carry than one that must constantly be displayed.

A brief complaint is a harmless way of letting off steam, but a habit of complaining keeps us exactly where we are. The next time you hear yourself starting a long grumble, pause and ask what single step you could take to improve the situation. Sometimes the answer is that there is nothing to be done, in which case the kindest option is to let it go.

Complaining feels productive because it is noisy, and because other people nod in sympathy and add complaints of their own. When the conversation is over, however, the problem is exactly as large as it was at the start, and we are a little more tired and a little more bitter. The satisfaction of being agreed with is a poor substitute for the satisfaction of having changed something.

When Maya catches herself complaining about the chaos of her filing system, she interrupts the grumble and asks what single step she could take this week. The answer, which is to spend fifteen minutes on Friday sorting one drawer, is so modest that it embarrasses her a little. Yet that quarter of an hour achieves more than a month of sighing, and she wonders how many of her complaints are really small tasks in disguise.

Some problems really cannot be solved, whether it is the weather, a long queue or a cancelled flight, and then the one step available is to accept that fact. It is perfectly healthy to say aloud that it is annoying, to share a sigh with a friend and then to put the matter down. The skill lies in telling the difference between a problem that deserves your effort and one that deserves only your patience.

Every morning a small group of colleagues, including Dev, gathers by the coffee machine to complain about the company, the schedule and the carpet. Maya used to join them eagerly, and she used to leave feeling bonded and slightly poisoned, but this morning she says kindly that she has a call to make and walks away. She does not judge them, and she does not lecture them, because she has simply decided where her coins will go.

For months the whole office has grumbled that the Monday meeting begins too early, and nobody has said so to the person who could change it. Maya finally asks Ines, politely and clearly, whether the meeting could start at ten, and Ines considers it for a moment and agrees. A complaint tells the world that something is wrong, whereas a request tells one particular person what would make it right.

Dev tells anyone who will listen that he is always unlucky, that bad things simply happen to him and that no one ever gives him a fair chance. Maya notices that the facts of her own life can be told in two ways, and that when she describes herself as the person who makes choices instead of the person who suffers them, she feels instantly stronger. The facts have not changed, but the narrator has, and the narrator turns out to matter a great deal.

Each night before bed Maya writes down three small things that went well that day, such as a kind word from a stranger, a warm shower or a joke that made her laugh aloud. The habit does not blind her to genuine problems, and she has no intention of pretending that everything is perfect. It simply puts her complaints in proportion by reminding her that the day contained more than its irritations.

Leo spends an entire lesson complaining that scales are boring, repetitive and pointless, and Ms Okafor lets him finish without a word. Then she asks him what song he most wants to play, and when he names it she shows him the very scale that runs through its middle. The complaint dissolves, because the dull exercise has become a bridge to something he actually wants.

Maya writes the words One step today on a small card and fixes it to her fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon. Whenever a complaint rises in her, she glances at the card and chooses a single action, however tiny, that would make the situation slightly better. Over the weeks the grumbles in her head grow quieter, not because life has become easier, but because she has learned to answer them with something to do.

We have become so afraid of boredom that we fill every spare second with a screen, and so we rarely discover what is going on inside our own heads. If you leave a few gaps in the day, you may begin to notice what you really think, what you really enjoy and what has been quietly worrying you. Those gaps are not wasted time, since they are where a good deal of self-knowledge is found.

In the supermarket queue Maya reaches for her phone with the speed of a reflex, as she has done in every queue for years. This time she stops herself, slides it back into her pocket and simply looks around at the shelves, the faces and the slow-moving line. It is uncomfortable for about a minute, and then it becomes almost interesting, like discovering a room in her own house that she had never entered.

On the long train ride home Maya looks out of the window without a screen, and for ten minutes she is thoroughly bored. Then, with no warning at all, the solution to a stubborn problem at work drifts into her mind, as though it had been waiting politely for the noise to stop. Boredom is not an empty room but a doorway, and the mind often does its best work when it is left alone.

For the first time in years Maya walks to the park without headphones, and the world arrives in layers that she had forgotten, from the birds overhead to the footsteps behind her and the distant bell of a bicycle. Her thoughts, freed from the constant stream of other people's voices, begin to speak up in a quieter and more personal tone. She had not realised how crowded her attention had been until she gave it a little silence.

Maya used to hurry through the washing-up with the news blaring in the background, treating it as a barrier between herself and the sofa. Tonight she does it slowly and with her whole attention, noticing the warmth of the water, the shine of the soap and the clean squeak of a glass. A dull task, she finds, becomes a small meditation when she stops wishing that she were somewhere else.

One weekend Maya decides to dedicate herself entirely to pleasure, so she fills it with pastries, films and a long shopping trip. Each treat is enjoyable at the time, but each one fades faster than the last, and by Sunday evening she is sitting among bags and boxes feeling strangely flat. Pleasure is a pleasant visitor, but it is a poor tenant, because it never stays long enough to make a home.

Pleasure is delightful, but it is also quick to fade, and anyone who pursues it exclusively will find that the satisfaction wears thinner each time. Meaning is built from a different material, since it comes from devoting your effort to something that matters beyond your own comfort. It is slower and sometimes harder, yet it leaves a far deeper feeling at the end of the day.

When Aunt Nora comes down with a bad cold, Maya gives up a free Sunday to cook a large pot of stew and carry it, still steaming, across town. It is tiring, it costs her an afternoon of painting, and nobody posts a picture of it, yet she walks home with a deep warmth that no pastry or film had given her the weekend before. Meaning is usually made of such plain things, which are time, effort and somebody else's wellbeing.

Raising a child, caring for an elderly parent or mastering a demanding craft is rarely relaxing, and anyone who describes it as constant joy is probably selling something. These labours are tiring, frustrating and often thankless, yet many of the people who give themselves to them would not exchange them for a life of ease. This is the strange arithmetic of meaning, in which the things that cost us the most are often the things that we would least like to lose.

Maya sits down with her notebook and makes two lists, one of the activities that leave her tired in a good way and one of those that leave her merely empty. The first list is short and includes painting, cooking for people she loves and talking honestly with a friend, while the second is long and full of scrolling. She cannot delete the second list from her life entirely, but she resolves to move a few of its hours across to the first.

Holding a grudge is rather like carrying a heavy stone around in order to prove to someone how badly they hurt you, while the other person is probably not even looking. Forgiveness does not mean pretending that the harm was acceptable, or that you must spend time with the person again. It simply allows you to put the stone down and spend your coins somewhere better.

Three years ago a colleague named Rob presented one of Maya's ideas as his own, and he was praised for it in front of the whole department. She has never forgiven him, and she carries the memory around like a polished stone, taking it out whenever she feels undervalued. The odd thing is that Rob left the company long ago and probably has not thought about the matter once since.

In the shower, on the train and sometimes even at dinner, Maya composes brilliant speeches that she will never deliver to Rob, each one sharper than the last. She wins every one of these imaginary arguments, but each victory costs her a handful of coins and leaves her more tired than before. The grudge is expensive to keep, and the only person paying the bill is the one who is holding it.

Mr Haddad listens to Maya's story over a glass of mint tea, turning an old pocket watch over in his fingers, and then he says something that she will remember for years. To forgive, he says, is not to declare that the wrong was acceptable, and it is not to invite the person back into your life, but only to stop paying interest on a debt that will never be repaid. The wrong remains a wrong, and Maya remains perfectly free to keep her distance from the man who committed it.

On a quiet evening Maya writes Rob a long and honest letter that says everything she has held back for three years, from the anger to the humiliation. She reads it once, folds it, and decides not to send it, because its purpose was never to change him but to let her put the weight down. Something tight in her chest loosens as the paper settles into the recycling bin, and she feels, for the first time in years, a little lighter.

Maya realises that although the new rule is working well, she is still carrying a secret list of every occasion on which Sam let her down. She imagines tearing it into small pieces and letting them fall, and she tells Sam about the list over dinner, making it sound much funnier than it felt. Sam laughs, apologises once more, and the friendship is lighter than it has been in a long time.

Last week Maya lost her patience and snapped at Dev in front of the whole team, and the memory has been scraping at her conscience ever since. Having learned to forgive other people's mistakes, she finds it a little easier to admit her own, so she walks to his desk and tells him plainly that she is sorry. Dev blinks, then smiles with visible relief, and admits that he had been dreading the next meeting.

A good apology has three parts, which are a clear statement of what you did, a plain expression of regret and an offer to repair the damage. It leaves out the little word but, which has a way of cancelling everything that was said before it, and it does not ask the other person to feel better at once. Maya has found that an apology of this sort costs a few uncomfortable minutes and earns a great deal of trust.

Maya still feels a hot flush of shame whenever she remembers a mistake from when she was twenty-two, when she let down a friend who needed her. She asks herself what she would say to a friend who confessed the same story, and she realises at once that she would be gentle, understanding and firm about the future. She decides to offer herself that same treatment, since the self she has to live with every day deserves to be treated at least as well as a stranger.

With her grudges put down and her apologies made, Maya notices that her mind has become less crowded, like a house from which someone has removed a lot of unnecessary furniture. At the end of each day she now has coins left over, and she spends them on painting, on friends and on sleep. Letting go, she concludes, is not a loss at all, but a kind of income.

A local band announces that it needs a new guitarist, and Leo, to everyone's surprise including his own, decides to audition. For three weeks he practises two songs every evening, polishing each chord change until the movements are almost automatic. He does not know whether he is good enough, but he knows that he has done the part that was his to do.

Leo sits in the corridor outside the rehearsal room with cold hands, a dry mouth and a heartbeat that he can hear in his ears. Maya, who has come to keep him company, reminds him gently that nervousness is only a signal and that it simply shows how much this matters to him. He nods, breathes slowly, and when his name is called he stands up more steadily than he had expected.

Leo walks into the rehearsal room, greets the three musicians waiting behind a battered drum kit, and begins his first song with fingers that tremble more than he would like. Halfway through the second he makes one clear mistake, hesitates, and then continues to the end without stopping, which is something that he could not have done a few months earlier. When the last chord fades, the room is quiet, and he realises that he is proud of himself no matter what they say.

Leo auditions for a local band, plays two songs with trembling fingers and is politely turned down the same afternoon. He feels dreadful for a day, then phones the band and asks what he should improve, and he starts working on exactly those things. Rejection is painful, but it is also a very direct and surprisingly generous kind of information that praise could never have provided.

Leo says very little on the bus ride home, and Maya, who has recently learned the value of not fixing things too quickly, does not try to cheer him up. She sits beside him in a companionable silence while he lets the disappointment be as large as it needs to be. Pain that is allowed to take its full size tends to pass more quickly than pain that is argued with, and by the time they reach his stop he has managed a small, rueful smile.

When Leo phones the band, the drummer is kind enough to give him three honest notes, which are to keep a steadier beat, to look up from the strings and to play fewer notes. One of them stings, because it describes exactly the habit he had been proudest of, yet he writes them all down without arguing. Rejection that arrives with specific information is a gift in an awkward wrapper, and he intends to unwrap it.

Maya explains to Leo that criticism arrives in three varieties, which are useful advice, matters of personal taste and remarks that are simply unkind. The first should be acted on, the second should be weighed and the third should be quietly dropped, however loudly it was said. Learning to sort feedback in this way protects you from two opposite mistakes, which are swallowing everything and rejecting everything.

Ines reads Maya's report carefully and tells her that it is clear and thorough but far too long, and Maya feels heat climbing into her face. Every defensive sentence in the world rushes to her tongue, yet she remembers that a feeling is not an order, takes one slow breath and says that she would like to hear more. The criticism is not an attack on her, and she is surprised to notice how much easier it is to listen once she has understood that.

Maya reminds herself that a poor report is not the same thing as a poor person, and that her worth does not rise and fall with every piece of work. The report can be cut in half, improved and handed in again, and in the meantime nothing fundamental about her has changed. People who cannot separate themselves from their work experience every criticism as an attack, whereas people who can separate them experience it as a service.

A month later Leo plays two songs at the open evening in a small cafe, keeping a steady beat, looking up at his listeners and leaving out half the notes that he would once have crammed in. Nobody offers him a contract, and no band calls the next morning, but a stranger stops him at the door to say how much she enjoyed it. He walks home understanding that the audition was never the point, since the music was, and the music is still his.

At the back of a cupboard Maya finds a ukulele, a pair of knitting needles, a Spanish grammar and a half-finished scarf, each the remains of a burst of enthusiasm that lasted about three weeks. She counts eight abandoned hobbies, and she is not ashamed so much as curious, since each began with such a hopeful purchase. Starting is easy and thrilling, and it was never the hobbies that failed her, but the absence of any decision to stay.

There is a surprising kind of freedom in deciding that this is the thing you will do, and in closing the other doors for a while. Those who sample everything for a few weeks never reach the depth that comes only from staying with a single pursuit through its dull middle. Commitment narrows your choices in the short term, but over the years it widens enormously what you are able to achieve.

Someone who keeps every door open never walks all the way through any of them, and spends the years standing in the hallway with a hand on first one handle and then another. Options feel like freedom, but each unused option continues to claim a small share of attention, whispering that something else might be better. The price of unlimited choice is the quiet and constant cost of not having chosen.

Maya decides to pick a single pursuit and to give it a full season before she judges whether it was a good choice. A farmer does not dig up the seeds after a week to check whether anything has happened, and a skill, in the same way, needs time in the dark before it shows above the ground. Patience is not a decoration added to commitment after the fact, but one of its main ingredients from the start.

To make her choice well, Maya spreads her old lists across the floor, which are her values, the struggles she accepts and the activities that leave her tired in a good way. She runs her finger down each page, and one item appears on all three, so clearly that it makes her laugh. The pages of her notebook, which once seemed like scattered experiments, now fit together like the steps of a single argument.

Weeks earlier Maya promised to watch Leo play at his school concert, and on the very same evening she receives an invitation to a glamorous party that she would love to attend. For a moment the two choices glitter side by side, but she remembers that a commitment is a decision made in advance for the days on which you will not feel like keeping it. She sits in the second row of the hall, applauding louder than anyone, and does not regret a minute.

Commitment does not mean that you are never allowed to stop anything, and Maya has no intention of becoming a prisoner of her own decisions. She puts the ukulele and the half-finished scarf into a box for the charity shop, and the act of saying goodbye on purpose feels very different from letting things fade out of neglect. The difference between quitting and drifting is that one is a choice, while the other is only a slow, guilty forgetting.

Dev has been dragging himself to a dull evening course for months, because he paid for the whole term in advance and cannot bear to waste it. Maya points out, as kindly as she can, that the money has gone whether he attends or not, and that the only sensible question is how he wants to spend his evenings from here on. Costs that have already been paid and cannot be recovered should not be allowed to vote on the future.

Maya thinks seriously about leaving her job, and after a week of honest reflection she concludes that most of what she values is there, including the people, the learning and the pay. What she needs to change is the shape of the work, so she asks Ines for fewer simultaneous projects and clearer hours, and Ines agrees to a trial. Commitment, she sees, is not always a matter of staying or leaving but of renegotiating the terms on which you stay.

Maya pays for a full year of painting classes and writes it in her notebook as her single new pursuit, with a firm line under it. She feels a small tremor of fear at the thought of all the other doors that she is closing, followed almost at once by a larger wave of relief. It turns out that a narrow path is much easier to walk than a wide field, because at every step she knows where to put her foot.

On her birthday Maya blows out the candles while her friends sing, and in the brief hush that follows she feels a small shock at how quickly another year has disappeared. The feeling is not sadness exactly, but a sharpening, as if someone had wiped a window that had been fogged for a very long time. She realises that she has been behaving as though there were an endless supply of years, and that nobody ever tells us how many there are.

Your time on earth is limited, and none of us knows exactly how much of it remains. This may sound gloomy, but the fact is what gives each choice about your attention its weight, since a thing that cannot be repeated is worth more than one that can. It is a gentle and perfectly sensible reason to begin spending your coins with a little more care, starting today.

A person who lives to the age of eighty will have about four thousand weeks in total, which is a number that sounds enormous until you draw each week as a small square on a long strip of paper. Maya does this one evening with a ruler, and the strip stretches across her table and turns out to be shorter than she expected. It is not a reason for panic, only for a calmer and more honest look at how those squares are being filled.

In Mr Haddad's small flat the shelves are crowded with old clocks, and every one of them shows a different time, which makes the room tick like a field full of crickets. He tells Maya, with a mild smile, that in his working life he mended nearly every kind of clock but never learned to mend time itself. What a clock-mender does learn, he says, is that every tick is spent whether anyone is watching or not.

Try to imagine yourself as a very old person sitting by a window and looking back over the years. Which of today's worries will seem faintly ridiculous from there, and which relationships, efforts and kindnesses will you be glad you put first? The answer is a more reliable guide to your priorities than any list of goals.

Maya asks Mr Haddad what he is most glad about when he looks back over his life, and he takes a long time to answer. He speaks about the people he loved, the neighbours he helped and the small jobs that he did with care, and he does not mention a single object that he owned or an award that he won. His answer is perfectly simple, and on the walk home it quietly rearranges her entire list of priorities.

Nobody enjoys thinking about the end of life, and there is no need to dwell on it gloomily, but a gentle awareness of it can be remarkably useful. Beside it, small irritations shrink, grand ambitions are weighed more honestly, and the people we love suddenly look more precious than our schedules. The purpose of remembering that time runs out is not to frighten ourselves, but to make us a little more awake.

Maya climbs a hill on the edge of the city one evening and looks down at the roofs, the tiny cars and the winding river lit by the setting sun. From up there the awkward email that worried her all of yesterday seems as small and distant as the traffic, and the argument about a parking space is simply invisible. Distance is a kind of wisdom, and she resolves to take a step back in her mind whenever a small thing begins to feel enormous.

For three years Maya has been meaning to phone an old school friend, and each time she has told herself that it would be easier next month. This evening, with the hill and Mr Haddad's clocks still fresh in her mind, she stops waiting for the perfect moment and simply dials the number. The conversation lasts an hour, and it begins with a small laugh, because her friend says that she was about to call her.

Time is spent one day at a time, and Maya realises that she has been thinking about the great questions of life without changing a single Tuesday. She therefore writes one meaningful thing in her notebook for the week ahead, which is a long visit to Mr Haddad, and she keeps the appointment. The great shape of a life is made of ordinary days, and these are the only ones that she is ever able to spend.

A list with forty priorities is not really a list but a pile, and a pile gives no guidance on what to pick up first. When everything is marked as important, nothing is, and the person carrying the heap tends to freeze or to grab whatever is nearest. Maya understands that she needs a list so short that she could recite it while waiting for a kettle to boil.

To choose her five, Maya draws three overlapping circles and labels them values, struggles and people, and then she fills each one slowly and honestly. Whatever appears in two or more of the circles is a strong candidate, while whatever appears in only one is held up to the light and questioned. The method is not scientific, but it forces her to choose by what matters rather than by what is loudest.

Maya sits down one evening and writes the five things she wants to give her best attention to, which are her health, her family, her friendships, one skill she wants to master and her honesty. She pins the list above her desk and promises herself that anything else will have to earn its place. It feels strange and a little selfish at first, and then, within a week or two, it begins to feel like enormous relief.

Whenever a new request, invitation or worry arrives, Maya glances up at the card above her desk and asks a single question, which is whether it serves one of her five lines. If it does, she gives it her full attention, and if it does not, she can let it go with a clear conscience. Decisions that used to take an hour of agonising now take about a minute, and the minutes add up to hours.

Once a week, perhaps on a quiet Sunday morning, take a few minutes to look back through your calendar and ask where your coins have actually gone. If the answer does not match the list on your wall, choose one small change for the coming week rather than rebuilding your whole life. Gentle, regular corrections work far better over a lifetime than the occasional dramatic overhaul that is abandoned within a month.

Maya's Sunday review has three questions, which are where her coins actually went, what gave her energy and what drained it, and which one thing she will change in the week ahead. She answers each of them in a single honest line, because she has learned that long reviews are the ones that never get done. The whole thing takes ten minutes, and it is the best ten minutes of her week.

On some days you will forget everything you have read here and find yourself worrying about trivial things, answering every message and comparing yourself with strangers. This is entirely normal, and there is no need to punish yourself for it. Simply notice what has happened, smile a little, and return to your list as soon as you remember.

A very busy month arrives at work, and Maya cannot possibly give all five lines of her card their usual share of time. Instead of throwing the card away in frustration, she shrinks two of the lines to a bare minimum and writes down the date on which they will grow again. A list of priorities is not a contract to be broken but a living plan that bends when life requires it, and it remains useful precisely because it bends.

Maya notices that on the days when she sleeps badly and skips meals, her coins seem to vanish much faster, and every small irritation grows into a crisis. Sleep, plain food and a daily walk are not glamorous, and no one will ever congratulate her on them, but they are the foundation on which every other choice is built. She decides that looking after the basics is not a distraction from what matters, but the first item on the list.

One lunchtime Dev tells Maya that she seems different, calmer and somehow harder to rattle, and he asks with real curiosity how she does it. She does not deliver a speech, and she does not claim to have discovered a secret, but she takes the card from her bag and shows him its five short lines. He reads them twice in silence, and then he asks whether she could help him write a few of his own.

One morning Maya reads her card as if a stranger had written it, and she notices that every line begins with the word my. It is a good card, and it has already made her life calmer, yet it contains no line that looks beyond her own circle of comfort. She has learned to spend her coins on purpose, and now she begins to wonder what a really generous purpose might be.

Of all the places where you could spend your attention, the most rewarding is usually something larger than your own comfort, such as a family, a neighbourhood or a cause you truly believe in. Such commitments give you a reason to continue when you are tired and a way of measuring your days that does not depend on applause. Such commitments, in short, turn ordinary effort into something that can truly be called meaning, even on the days that feel plain.

Maya joins the community garden for a single hour every Saturday morning, and the work is simple, muddy and delightfully unimportant to anyone except the people doing it. Within a month she knows the names of a dozen neighbours she had never spoken to, and she can tell which of the tomato plants is sulking. The hour is a small gift to the neighbourhood, but she soon suspects that she is receiving the larger share.

Leo agrees to teach a seven-year-old from the next street how to play his first chord, and he is astonished by how much he has to explain. The effort of putting each movement into words makes him understand his own playing more deeply, and when the small fingers finally produce a clear sound, the boy's delight is worth more than any applause he has received. Something that began as a favour has turned into one of Leo's best lessons.

The news is full of enormous problems that Maya cannot solve, and she discovers that caring about all of them equally produces only a sense of helplessness. She decides to choose one cause within her reach, to follow it carefully and to act on it in a modest way, and then to let the rest of the headlines pass without guilt. It is not that the other troubles do not matter, but that a person who tries to hold the whole world will eventually drop it.

Let us gather the main ideas into one place before you close this book. Choose your struggles deliberately, pick values that you can practise yourself, accept responsibility for your response, test your beliefs, say no kindly and compare yourself only with who you were before. None of these ideas is complicated, but each of them takes a lifetime of patient practice, and none of them is ever fully finished.

Dev tries to write his own card, but he keeps adding lines until the list is a page long, and then he declares that he has failed before he has begun. Maya laughs kindly and tells him that this is a practice and not a switch, and that she still forgets her own card for several days at a time. Nobody becomes wise in a single evening, but anyone can begin again, and beginning again is most of the skill.

Maya writes a short letter to the person she will be a year from now, and she seals it in an envelope marked with the date on which it may be opened. She writes down what she has learned, what she is proud of and what she hopes will still be true, and she ends it with a plain promise to go on choosing. Putting the future into words makes it feel less like something that happens to her and more like something that she is building.

On a quiet morning Maya sits at the same kitchen table where, months ago, she first counted her coins and felt overwhelmed. The bag is no larger than it was then, and no wizard has refilled it, but she now knows what she wants to buy with every coin. She finishes her tea slowly, picks up her bag, and goes out to spend the day.

Maya still has the same demanding job, the same crowded city and the same modest purse of coins each morning, yet she spends them with remarkable deliberation. She cares about far fewer things than she used to, and she cares about those things much more fully. That, in essence, is the entire secret of this book, and it is yours to use from today.
